introFa: کتاب «The Red and the Black» نوشته Stendhal یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

REVIEWS 173 RED AND BLACK IN THE NEW WORLD Black Africans and Native Americans : Color, race and caste in the evolution of Red- Black peoples. By JACK D. FORBES. Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1988. Pp. 345. £35-00. African Presence in Early America. Edited by IVAN VAN SERTIMA. New Brunswick, New Jersey: Transaction Books, 1987. Pp. 338. $15.00 paperback. Distributed in U.K. by Clio Distribution Services, Oxford. The prevailing assumption concerning the history of trans-Atlantic relations is that the only movement has been that of Europeans and Africans from the Old World to the New. Jack Forbes, himself a Native American, challenges this view by assembling all the evidence for instances of Americans migrating in the other direction, from ancient Eskimos accidentally carried to the British Isles by the Gulf Stream, to modern settlers of American ancestry. His larger project is to reclaim for Americans at least part of the cultural influence, in the Americas and elsewhere, generally attributed to 'blacks', assumed to be of exclusively African or Afro-European ancestry. To this end Forbes exhaustively examines texts from the Old and New Worlds, in many European languages but principally English, Spanish and Portuguese, to show that the terms applied to people of colour were essentially descriptive rather than taxonomic. It is only in the eighteenth and increasingly in the nineteenth century, with the development of colonial systems of social stratification, that colour terms were simplified, standardized, and employed to classify people by their presumptive ancestry and thus their assigned social destiny. Forbes rightly insists that one should not read such texts in terms of modern race classifications. Approximately half of the book examines the use of such terms as ' mulatto' and 'mestizo' in the Americas, to show that in many instances the individuals so labelled were either wholly or partly of American ancestry. Forbes' conclusion is that Native Americans were not caused totally to disappear by conquest, genocide or other more or less violent forms of displacement at the hands of immigrants. On the contrary, 'American survivors and African survivors have merged together to create the basic modern populations of much of the Greater Caribbean and adjacent mainland regions' (p. 270). 'The ancestry of modern-day Americans, whether "black" or "Indian" in appearance, is often (or usually) quite complex indeed. It is sad that many such persons have been forced by racism into arbit- rary categories which tend to render their ethnic heritage simple rather than com- plex. It is now one of the principal tasks of scholarship to replace the shallow one-dimensional images of non-whites with more accurate multi-dimensional portraits' (p. 271). It is a provocative thesis, pushed a little too hard at times, as a revisionist is entitled to do. Along the way, Forbes reviews the evidence for pre-Columbian African arrivals in the Americas and finds much of the evidence unconvincing. His methodological scruples are not shared by Van Sertima and his colleagues, whose interpretations of history are predicated on precisely the modern racism that Forbes sets aside. A racist is one who believes that the human species was originally divided into 'Black, Yellow and White racial varieties' (Van Sertima, p. 10), that the present variability of human populations is attributable to later miscegenation, but that in any mixture the traits of the original races remain discretely identifiable. Polish physical anthropologists, upon whom Van Sertima relies, follow what was once the standard practice, abandoned by everybody else since the discovery of genetics, of classifying any collection of bones as black, white or yellow on the basis of a

174 JOURNAL OF AFRICAN HISTORY number of measurements, particularly of the skull. Culture is treated in the same way: a given collection of traits can be classified as black, white or yellow, and the results combined with cranial 'evidence' to create remarkable configurations that, in the mind of the racist, can only be explained by the long-distance migrations of small but formidable groups. Africanists will be familiar with this set of assumptions, which until about i960 entitled European historians to disassemble African culture into traits of which they approved, and called Caucasoid or Hamitic, and the rest, which could be considered native to Africa. Van Sertima (educated, he says, at SOAS) and col- leagues use the same methods in the service of a sort of black cultural imperial- ism, which at its most ambitious appropriates the entirety of American culture from the paleolithic onwards. Rummaging through the whole of African and the whole of American culture, the authors have no difficulty in developing a list of parallels to impress the inexperienced. Readers whose imagination has hitherto been limited to the idea of Meroitic princes escaping to the west with the secret of kingship in their knapsacks will be astonished by the scale of the migrations here proposed to account for these parallels. My favourite, which is based in part on 'some excellent Jewish heads' to be seen among the terracottas of Nok, Nigeria, has Jews escaping from Persian persecution in Egypt in 525 B.C. and making their way to Brazil with the help of Nigerian navigators (pp. 65-6). Haverford College, WYATT MACGAFFEY Pennsylvania THE ECOLOGY OF SURVIVAL The Ecology of Survival. Case Studies from Northeast African History. Edited by DOUGLAS H. JOHNSON and DAVID M. ANDERSON. London and Boulder: Lester Crook Academic Publishing and Westview Press, 1988. Pp. xii + 339. No price given. Johnson and Anderson have put together a timely, solid book. It has immediate claims on several constituencies. Scholars of north-eastern Africa will find that it addresses major questions of human ecology, mode of production and ethnic formation. Methodologically, it is at the cutting edge of both history and anthro- pology. Its concern with drought and famine is central to the contemporary Africanist agenda. The collection's announced purpose is to examine 'The historical continuities of ecological change and ecological stress in northeast Africa'. Pleading that a truly satisfactory resolution of current crises will have to incorporate the wider understanding of social context and historical perspective which their collection embodies, the editors distance themselves from the 'Africa in crisis' school of literature. This is a creative collection, first of all in its emphasis on north-eastern Africa as a region. Among scholars of the area there seems to be a growing interest in the region as such, but this is one of the first books to bring that consciousness before the wider public, even if its coverage is less comprehensive than the editors might have wished. North-eastern Africa, in this instance, consists of Sudan (4 case studies), Kenya (3 cases), Ethiopia (2 cases) and Uganda (1). Somalia is the notable omission. The editors argue that with respect to their mode of subsistence production the region is characterized by societies each of which exists along its own peculiar continuum inclusive of cultivation, pastoralism, and hunting and gathering.
